#### **Kaiowá and Guarani School Education and**

#### **Interculturality: Tensions, Dialogues, and the**

#### **Strengthening of Traditional Knowledge**

In this last part, having previously reflected on Kaiowá and
Guarani sustainability and spiritual technologies, I proceed to a
discussion of these traditional knowledges of my people, from
my own point of view as an educator and tireless fighter for a
school education specific to my people.
First, it must be pointed out that perspectives on
intercultural education are always in dispute, and today they are
being challenged through the struggles of indigenous peoples,
aiming at a transformation of the ways in which knowledge is
constructed, one grounded in traditional knowledge and
respectful of the self-determination of peoples.
In this sense, this chapter aims to reflect on the specific
features of intercultural efforts for indigenous peoples, their
tensions, dialogues, and disputes, in order to raise questions and
aspects related to this process in school education in the
Panambizinho tekoha. At the same time, I have also cast an eye
over the experiences of other indigenous peoples built as
community educational spaces.
The proposal is a reflection from the standpoint of a Kaiowá
researcher and educator on intercultural processes, a bias of
interculturality that has often served as a shallow discourse and
as an institutional tool for maintaining the colonizer's policy,
since it continues to privilege only one culture, that of the karaí
(white/non-indigenous people). I seek to discuss how
interculturality can be used as a tool strengthened by
communities and built on the ground of the territories. For this,
my starting point is the questioning reflection of the indigenous
103
researcher Célia Xakriabá: "How do we turn the weapon that
colonized us into a space of subversion as well?" (CORREA,
2018, p. 165).
The diversity of peoples and knowledges is one of the great
wonders of the world; this exuberant diversity makes possible
the coexistence of cultures and peoples of different ethnic and
geographic origins. However, these relations of exchange
between distinct cultures generate two-way transformations that
may or may not favor the continued existence of the cultures
involved, since there is a relation of power imposed by the
modern colonial system, which marginalizes peoples who
organize themselves socially and territorially in multiple ways. In
this way, cultural exchange, known as interculturality, when it
occurs between indigenous cultures and Western culture, favors
only one side, that is, the side of the whites.
The ethnocentric and Eurocentric reading of the world has
left us a trail of violence, exploitation, and dispossession where
intercultural education is concerned. We were led to believe that
the only way to build intercultural knowledge is from the
knowledge of Western peoples; and this is why I understand that
the challenges to be faced in building an Indigenous school
education that is both intercultural and just for us are enormous.
Maintaining the structure of looking at Indigenous peoples
as “the others” and positioning itself as a dominant system that
masks this marginalization, interculturality has often been called
“official” and is sustained by a matrix that subordinates other
forms of knowledge and socio-territorial organization; it must be
reiterated that this same interculturality was established by the
State and by the knowledge of the karaí.
Top-down interculturality is a monocultural interculturality;
it is a denial of multiplicity, seeking a hegemony and a
104
coloniality of knowledge and power that is also expressed in
schools, universities, and institutes, making Eurocentric
knowledge and concepts predominate. The same occurs with the
perspective of official interculturality, as the author Quijano
(1992) affirms.
Coloniality is related to the pattern of power in the process
of domination through a colonization of the imaginary and
through the imposition of a paradigm considered universal, as
part of European rationality. In light of this, the author Edson
Kaiapó (2019) emphasizes that the school, under national
ideology, historically created ‘the myth of the generic Indigenous
person,’ represented by a set of stereotypes that reproduce
structural racism and constant marginalization.
In this condition, the State creates mechanisms to control
diversity through this interculturality grounded in the same
structures of power, without even seeking to create possibilities
for policies and actions that combat violations and violence
against Indigenous cultures. The law of the karaí, that is, the
1988 Federal Constitution, recognized the importance of Brazil's
multicultural character, as well as full respect for the original
right of Indigenous peoples to their traditional territories, as
Daniel Munduruku shows:
The current Federal Constitution addresses the rights of
Indigenous peoples in a transversal, broad, and innovative
manner, recognizing that the need for special legal protection for
Indigenous peoples lies in cultural diversity and not in civil
incapacity, which made possible the drafting, in the years that
followed, of abundant infra-constitutional Indigenous legislation,
granting these minorities the right to ethnic, linguistic, and
cultural diversity, without prejudice to their prerogatives as
Brazilian citizens (MUNDURUKU, 2012, p. 37)
105
In this context, a series of initiatives began to be adopted for
Indigenous School Education, aiming at a differentiated
education (CAVALCANTE, 2017). However, it is important to
note that, most of the time, actions guided by a bureaucratic and
institutional vision predominated, through a perspective of
interculturality that privileges only the interests of the karaí and
of the Brazilian State itself, to the detriment of the agendas and
demands of Indigenous peoples.
Thus, although it enables dialogue and a certain notion of
tolerance between different peoples and knowledges, this
education does not present itself as an interculturality grounded
in the valuing of traditional knowledge and spiritual
technologies, still less in the sense of an interculturality of a
contra-colonial character that is attentive to the struggles of these
peoples.
This process has been gradually questioned in recent
decades by curricular proposals in Indigenous schools, as the
number of Indigenous women and men teachers has grown,
with the orientation of valuing and strengthening the traditions
of Native Peoples (KAIAPÓ, 2019).
The increase in the number of Indigenous educators is
fundamental for reflecting on Indigenous protagonism through
entry into universities, which for Gersem Baniwa Luciano marks
“this new era of the vision and attitude of Indigenous peoples in
Brazil” (LUCIANO, 2012, p. 137). The author emphasizes that:
In the last 30 years, Indigenous peoples in Brazil, in my
understanding, made this decision to invest in education. And the
very strong arrival at university is part of this wager: school can
be an important instrument for the present and the future of these
peoples, in every respect, whether for greater interaction with the
surrounding world, with the non-Indigenous world as broadly as
possible, which shows the great interest in dialogue and
106
coexistence, but there are also specific interests, such as
improving living conditions in the villages (LUCIANO, 2012, p.
137)
Unlike the vision of the karaí and the perspective of
institutional bureaucracy, the vision of Indigenous peoples
regarding education is multiple and differs in that there exists
both traditional Indigenous education and Indigenous school
education. Kaiowá and Guarani Indigenous Education, our own
system of education, always begins in the space of the home, of
the domestic fire, in festivals and celebrations, where we learned
to do things alongside our elders, learning above all to pray and
to relate to the spiritual world. It was always the elders, mothers,
and fathers who taught the children and the younger ones. In
this collective space of the home we also learned many things
about the kokue (cultivated field).
For us, the Guarani and Kaiowá, especially the elders, we
understand the cultivated field not as suffering, but as leisure. It
is there that food is born. It is where we can teach our children
our way of being. So, the cultivated field is for us leisure and not
work (in the sense of punishment that work carries in the
Western concept). What differentiates us from this concept of the
white man is that the cultivated field, for us, is leisure, is
happiness (PERALTA, 2017, p. 4).
But when it comes to observing the format of Indigenous
School Education, one perceives that it is still guided, for the
most part, by the ideas and perspectives of the karaí and the
State, turning the intercultural proposal into an unequal, unjust,
and, worse, colonizing process. From this standpoint, I, as a
Kaiowá Indigenous educator and researcher, am quite concerned
about this predominance of State interests and the impacts this
has on our knowledge, which has already been greatly
weakened, violated, and marginalized by the Brazilian State. The
107
school itself wanted to destroy our knowledge. All the
knowledge we have kept continues to be violated and may be
lost if we do not change the tensions and contradictions
propagated by the karaí way of being.
The authors Ramalho and Leite (2020) point out that the
establishment and construction of the intercultural school
occurred in a way that maintained the exercise of preserving
State interests, through a colonizing character and an attempt at
whitening that gives little value to the cultures, languages,
traditions, and rights of Indigenous peoples over their territories.
This process immensely affected our ways of sharing knowledge,
where many peoples nearly lost their language, many lost their
songs, their prayers, and when you lose the language you lose
the whole root that surrounds ethnicity.
In an article written years ago, I pointed to this expropriation
of knowledge and the violence of the non-Indigenous way of
being toward our people:
We have watched much of the Indigenous knowledge that
prepared the remedies used to cure humanity become the object
of a science that ignores our importance in this process of
systematizing knowledge. The most absurd thing of all this is
seeing that we were expropriated of our knowledge as a result of
an inhumane domination that has inflicted upon us a series of
restrictions on the living conditions of Indigenous people,
stemming from this contact that was, for us, unequal and abusive
(Peralta, 2017, p. 5)
In this context, there are still various difficulties that
permeate the school, such as the silencing of the stories told by
Indigenous peoples themselves within school curricula, with a
colonial view and the mythification and folklorization of native
cultures predominating. This is evident both in the fact that we
still have non-Indigenous teachers in community schools, and in
108
the marginalization of traditional knowledge, since teaching
materials coming from the State end up reproducing the same
logic. The lack of strengthening of the protagonism of literature
and materials by Indigenous researchers in schools is a factor
that allows this continuum of marginalization to persist.
As an educator I am quite concerned about this, about what
interculturality seen from a “mono” view can go on causing us,
the native peoples. Because it is the elders, the men and women,
who ensure that we still have our language and our songs,
having managed to guard them with great care and never
opening up so that the white man could discover what we know.
It must be said that when one culture meets another, this
could be considered an interculturality, but what kind of
interculturality is this? This is the great crux of the question that
I raise here: Is interculturality my desiring to know the
knowledge of the other? The other knowing my knowledge?
Because each one has their own knowledge.
The problem does not lie in sharing our knowledge as
different peoples; we have always done this as humanity.
However, when this is established from a relationship of a
colonizing, hierarchical, and centralizing character, as the State
and white culture do, it generates many problems for
marginalized groups. The ignorance of the karaí reko (the white
man's way of life) institutes in the school an intercultural
character that ends up reproducing practices and movements
that fully impact the way of being and living of Indigenous
peoples.
But I believe it is possible to destroy this notion of school in
this hierarchical format and to think of it instead as a tool
through which we can fight for a communal space, in which
interculturality is carried out on the basis of our own peoples. I
109
see that few of us, teachers, actually practice this interculturality
built from the valuing of traditional knowledge, of our
Indigenous science. Perhaps we end up saying we are doing
interculturality, but we end up only translating the white man's
knowledge.
In many Indigenous schools there are various events shaped
like karaí events, such as the June festival, the graduation
ceremony, the Indigenous clothing parade, all in the white man's
model. And honestly, I do not know if this is interculturality.
White people talk about “interacting,” but when we interact
within this white model, the karaí culture is so colonizing that
we end up forgetting our own. Now I put this in question: How
many of our important traditional events and rituals are held
and taught in the Indigenous school? Are we not making room
for the marginalization of our traditional ways?
The intercultural attempts within Kaiowá and Guarani
Indigenous School Education, in the format in which they have
been carried out and conceived, along a single path where the
karaí devise things alone and then present the finished project to
the Indigenous peoples, is a process understood by our peoples
as an inefficient model doomed to failure, besides perpetuating
the colonizer's ideal. Therefore, even with some new attempts
that have been thought out and theorized, such as, for example,
the perspective of critical interculturality as opposed to the
functional perspective (CAVALCANTE, 2017), the Kaiowá and
Guarani still do not feel fully included when it comes to building
fairer and more dignified intercultural knowledge.
As I have emphasized, these dimensions of interculturality
and their historical impacts on our people concern me. I see that
this karaí interculturality can bring us a profound betrayal; we
give an extra dose of medicine and end up with deep and
devastating side effects.
110
From this perspective, I agree with the author Gersem
Baniwa Luciano (2012), when he stresses that, above all, it is
necessary to deconstruct the notions and concepts that
inferiorize our peoples and that hierarchize the different kinds of
knowledge taught in school, so that it is urgent to undo
colonizing ideas, in addition to carrying out a process of “true
de-education, that is, learning to recognize the mistakes learned
in school itself” (LUCIANO, 2012, p. 141).
Building another form of education aimed at destroying the
colonization of knowledge is fundamental to opening new
spaces and political-epistemological axes for rethinking
interculturality, from the standpoint of freedom and respect for
other cultures, epistemologies, and forms of knowledge
construction, as the author Aníbal Quijano (1992) emphasizes.
This type of model brought by the white man ends up being
imposed on us, Indigenous educators, sometimes without our
having any real notion of the effects it may cause and has already
caused. So I remain quite concerned, and we need to think much
more about what to do with interculturality. I also understand
that we Indigenous people do not need to be intercultural about
everything, all the time.
But we are contaminated by things from outside, such that
we have already been through destruction, through various
kinds of ‘ends,’ and now we are gaining awareness of the effects,
even though we have always resisted every process of
dispossession of life, of our territories, and of our knowledge. So
I remain quite concerned about interculturality, but I also see
that if we approach interculturality with respect we can build a
more peaceful good way of living, teko porã (the good way of
living) and teko vy'a (the way of being happy).
I agree once again with Gersem Baniwa Luciano (2012),
when the author relates that the school institution was
111
historically imposed on Indigenous peoples as an integrationist
and nationalist project, but was permanently confronted and
resignified by our peoples as a tool that enables a less
asymmetrical dialogue.
Thus, in seeking to confront and resignify the school, it is
necessary to place our Indigenous knowledge in transit as the
central axis for cultivating a differentiated school. This allows the
school to gradually be transformed into an instrument for
valuing orality, the knowledge of the eldest people, and the
valuing of each people's own ways of knowing and doing
education based on their own way of being and existing, which
in many cases has moved toward valuing Indigenous languages
and the oral knowledge of the elders.
As our relative Baniwa teaches us, only when we strengthen
this will a fair and dignified intercultural education be possible,
one in which conventional school pedagogies can dialogue
symmetrically and coexist with Indigenous pedagogies
(LUCIANO, 2012). This is a proposal for a fair and symmetrical
dialogue, so that Indigenous knowledge is recognized as
scientific, and so that there is an understanding of the
educational process as a trajectory that goes beyond the
possibilities and limitations of school walls, extending across the
whole territory.
As emphasized by the Indigenous author Célia Xakriabá
Correa (2018), many traditional women and men teachers say
that the school needs to be an interesting place for students, one
that should be grounded in the community's knowledge for life,
as well as valuing the experiences we live in the territory, where
the student needs to understand the inseparability of the body
from the territory.
112
That is why I also understand that interculturality can bring
the possibility of sharing knowledge with respect, since I believe
that when I can know and respect the culture of the other, this
allows another way of thinking and doing interculturality to be
built. As our relative Xakriabá says, “The intercultural
experience produces a displacement (or a relocation) of
thought” (CORREA, 2018, p. 165). Thus, I can continue being
myself, without being the other, without wanting to be the other,
and without the other imposing itself on me. From this
standpoint, Célia Xakriabá Correa (2018) points out:
As happens for the most part in academic production, the
teaching materials that reach our schools always privilege
theories produced at the center. It is as if the culture of the other
were stronger; there is a great fading and devaluing of
Indigenous students in the academic environment. Some students
go to university and are not considered producers, authors, and
interlocutors of knowledge in that setting. But there needs to be a
reverse process, which is what I call indigenization. Why not
indigenize the other? Why not quilombolize, peasant-ize the
other? That would be to exercise what is proposed by the very
concept of interculturality (CORREA, 2018, p. 19).
So, interculturality is important, but I think: to what extent is
it important for a people who have already endured five
hundred and twenty-two years of suffocation and violations? My
concern is with not allowing the white man to erase our culture,
with not allowing the school to erase our culture. I, as a teacher,
have to think a great deal about what I want to do with
interculturality. If interculturality is a place of respect, sometimes
when we want to respect too much or want to cure a person too
quickly, we end up giving an extra dose of medicine and it ends
up killing. In this sense, interculturality cannot be forced.
When I think about interculturality, I understand that it is
important, a necessary good, but the question is how to build
113
this concept collectively within the school. How are we going to
build this dialogically and collectively? For there to be
interculturality there have to be two cultures, and when they
meet, what will happen? They have to dialogue. In this dialogue,
to what extent can the other culture have my knowledge? And to
what extent can I have knowledge of the other culture?
If it is not built in a respectful, dialogical, and collective
manner, it will continue to be a hierarchical, unequal process
with many impacts on Indigenous peoples. From this
perspective, the distrust our peoples feel toward interculturality
can be understood, since the karaí worldview is not confluent
with the native Kaiowá and Guarani cosmoperception; on the
contrary, they are opposed. The quilombola intellectual Nêgo
Bispo warns that “confluence is the law that governs the
relationship of coexistence among the elements of nature and
teaches us that not everything that comes together
mixes” (SANTOS, 2015, p. 87).
In this same sense, the Indigenous intellectual of the
Kaingang people, in his doctoral thesis, reflects that “the white
man thinks of education as the best job, high wages, and
understands nature as merchandise” (EMILIANO, 2020). Thus,
the limitations of the white intercultural model are questioned
by us, the Kaiowá and Guarani. To think of interculturality from
the community base and from the valuing of traditional
knowledge, it is necessary to say clearly that there is knowledge
that we do not want to share with the karaí.
We do not want to show all our secrets of spiritual
technology; this is a memory that the guardians, the elders of my
people, both men and women, kept for a whole lifetime so that
white people would not usurp it. What we want to share with
the karaí are some aspects of mutual learning about coexistence
with nature, the relationship with the cultivated field and how
114
we build a cultivated field, what the methodology of our
people's traditional cultivated field is like, and what it means to
be sustainable from our point of view. This we can share so that
white people can learn and rethink their way of being and living.
We can also listen to what the methodology of white people
is like in their fields. We can learn what the white man thinks he
does right and what may seem wrong to us. This is dialogue; we
do not accept imposition. We can discuss how and why white
people destroy the land, and also see how they work the land.
For example, to recover a territory, let us discuss how the Kaiowá
and Guarani reclaim territory and seek to restore the life of the
land. Let us think together about how to restore and keep the
environment healthy. Let us observe how the white man restores
the environment, or whether he only causes damage. Let us
reflect on why they use that fertilizer and why we use this one.
These are important points for thinking about interculturality.
Another question relates to a point already raised in the text:
so how do we go about this horizontal dialogue? On the premise
that not everything can be intercultural. My fear is that our
studies may open gaps that further impact our ways of living.
Will the school be able to keep our language alive for another
five hundred years? Keep our culture alive for another five
hundred years? Will the school, through interculturality, manage
to do this? So I remain quite concerned, but I believe in fair and
respectful dialogue.
In contrast to intercultural discourses, we, Indigenous
peoples, desire an education that is liberating, that emancipates,
that is in keeping with our life, our culture, our spirituality, and
our histories and trajectories as peoples. It is in this respect that
dimensions of our political struggle are also inserted. This
process involves reflecting on how peoples decide the themes
and matters involved in the dynamics of education. Hence the
115
importance of thinking about our own politics, since it
presupposes the condition for a teaching-learning process
appropriate to our sociocultural points of view.
This differentiated education is a longstanding agenda and
demand of the Indigenous Movement, and among the Kaiowá
and Guarani it emerges with the Movement of Indigenous
Women and Men Teachers (MPGK), as a space of continuous
training and political action, premised on the struggle for the
right to a different kind of training, one that values traditional
knowledge.
This movement, which operates from within Indigenous
school education, has strengthened the emergence of new
Indigenous leaders and teachers with a new Kaiowá and
Guarani identity, based on the reclaiming of traditional cultural
values and the knowledge of other cultures, in a critical and
reflective manner, as the Kaiowá researcher Eliel Benites
explains:
These are contexts of deconstruction and reconstruction of values
and traditional identities, spaces of continuous training, in which
the traditional Kaiowá and Guarani way of being is articulated
with new postures, along with the construction of the strategies
necessary for political confrontation, with a view to realizing the
projects and dreams of Indigenous teachers (BENITES, 2014, p.
18-19).
Our education is born of the community and prioritizes our
own historical, geographical, and sociological processes, our
territorial struggles, and our own knowledge. Political self-
determination contributes to this end, to our managing our own
education ourselves, selecting the kinds of knowledge that
should be built and shared in community schools. In this way,
starting from ourselves, the school and another, possible
interculturality can become a reflective space and action
116
grounded in Kaiowá and Guarani values. From this, I want to set
down a marker that Indigenous knowledge and sciences are
fundamental to another way of thinking about education and to
putting an end to the Eurocentric colonization of knowledge, as
set out in a text of my own authorship:
With this, I want to demonstrate that our traditional knowledge is
capable of bringing answers to many of the questions that society
of today requires, for it is important to understand that we share
in this society; we are all on the same road, that is, we are part of
the same universe and must care for it (PERALTA, 2017, p. 9)
For our relative Célia Xakriabá, thinking about
interculturality with these meanings allows us to revisit our
educational practices, not in a superficial and artificial way, but
in an engaged way, experiencing the culture of other subjects, in
interaction:
It is no longer fitting to work with a curricular thinking such as
“disciplinarization”; we need, on the contrary, to question this
model of uniformization, which makes us always take as our
starting point segmentation, in an expectation (which often does
not come true) of reaching the whole. In indigenizing educational
practices, the proposal is the opposite: the invitation is to start
from the whole, from those that are our deep roots, to arrive at
the small details, these, thought of always as practices that lead
us to act in the world in an active, creative, and subversive way
whenever necessary (CORREA, 2018, p. 58).
And this process can only be built in a horizontal and
communitarian way, in which we take ownership of the schools
located in our territories, based on our own ways of reclaiming
this space. At the same time, it opens up paths that break with
the centralism and hierarchy that has always characterized
institutional and bureaucratic spaces. From this perspective, the
construction of knowledge is a process elaborated on the ground
of the village, drawing on the theoretical-methodological
117
potential of communities and the praxis of collective subjects
who question the colonizing role imposed by institutions.
In this way, Indigenous thought and its counter-hegemonic
practices sow an interculturality that recognizes and values the
diversity of epistemologies and the multiplicity of worlds and
forms of knowledge as an emancipatory instrument of discourse
and praxis, as pointed out by the author Jorge Viaña (2009).
It is a fact that this entire process has been built through
great struggle, for we know that in these five hundred and
twenty-two years, everything that the Original Peoples have
reclaimed and won as original rights came through much
resistance, and not because the State was willing to respect the
Original Peoples. We know it is a long journey, but we know that
a territorialized education is the key to strengthening our
peoples and communities, transforming educational spaces.
As the author Célia Xakriabá teaches us, thinking about a
territorialized education means starting from interaction with
the territory, and not “merely adding the knowledge produced in
the territory into the school, in such a way that this interaction is
committed, above all, to the question of the territory, and is
operated only from within it” (CORREA, 2018, p. 166).

##### **Other Possible Experiences for a Territorialized and**

##### **Community-Based Education**

For us, Original Peoples, in the multiplicity of peoples that
we are, education needs to be built from within our own
communities, in the territories where we live, and with the
collective agendas and strategies that strengthen our self-
determination and educational autonomy. That is why we fight
for a differentiated and intercultural education, as discussed
earlier, one that truly values horizontal dialogue and our
118
traditional knowledge. It is this movement that allows for the
gradual realization of a territorialized education, sustained by
the original matrix and by the ancestral struggle to defend our
wisdoms, our collectivities, and our ways of thinking/acting in
the world.
In parallel with Indigenous school education, we, the
Kaiowá and Guarani, have also built other experiences in our
communities, proposing other educational processes aimed at
strengthening collectivity and traditional knowledge. These
spaces are not institutional spaces, but our own spaces, raised up
by the community itself, constituting a dynamic of education
that is an alternative to the intercultural model implemented by
the State. These experiences take up once more the strengthening
of our own ways of organizing and propose an interculturality
conceived from our own way of being and living.
These proposals do not present themselves as an immediate
solution to all the problems caused by the karaí, but rather are
expressed as a path for thinking about new possibilities for the
construction of knowledge in community. They are experiences
of Indigenous, original education that drive individual and
collective emancipation.
Among our Kaiowá and Guarani people, one of the
important experiences takes place in the tekoha Panambizinho,
in the sacred space of Xiru Karai, known as an experimental
village-school, built since 2010. In this space we combine the
management of diverse plants, diversifying and keeping together
various cultivated species, in processes grounded in what I call
spiritual technology, valuing our knowledge, since the Kaiowá
and Guarani are traditionally farmers and have always produced
rich gardens and fields, which even fed many of the colonizers
(PERALTA, 2017).
119
The authors Monfort and Gisloti (2020) classify these
community experiences as actions built from ancestral
knowledge, and from Kaiowá and Guarani practices and
knowledge, as spheres of potential for processes of ecological
restoration, fundamental to territorial struggles and to new ways
of knowing-and-doing education and politics. The energies of
Kaiowá and Guarani pedagogy are related to the place where
one lives and the place where one is, opening new horizons for
thinking about collective paths of emancipation.
The project still has little support from Indigenous School
Education, but it is a fundamental project for Kaiowá and
Guarani pedagogy, and one that could make a great contribution
to the schools located in the villages. Although Xiru Karaí is
different from Indigenous School Education, the school
institution has much to learn from the autonomous spaces that
exist in the community and should value dialogue between these
experiences. The school must be open to strengthening the
community and the struggle of the people themselves, and not
be at the service of a system that has always oppressed the
Original Peoples.
Another experience that emerges among us, Kaiowá and
Guarani, is the community space Kurundua, in the Jaguapiru
village, one of the villages that make up the Dourados
Indigenous Reserve. The Kurundua space, built from the
community's political self-determination, was organized by a
Ñandesy and a Ñanderu as a community space aimed at
strengthening traditional knowledge through sharing between
different generations.
The territorial organization of the Indigenous Reserves
imposed a broad process of precarization within an extremely
reduced space, contrary to the possibility of living well, of bem
viver. Resisting this, one of the principles of this community
120
space is to strengthen collectivity through the Ñanderu and
Ñandesy, even amid the difficulties within the Indigenous
Reserve.
Another important experience is the Native Seedling
Nursery of the Ñandejara Pólo Municipal Indigenous School, in
the Teý’ikuê village, in the municipality of Caarapó, which began
its activities in 1997, with the proposal of producing native
seedlings for the restoration of springs and forests. The project is
linked to the Experimental Unit, which began its activities in
2001 for the management of cultivation practices, animal raising,
and the conservation of the region's microwatersheds, based on
Kaiowá and Guarani knowledge, with a view to the
agroecological and agroforestry system, as demonstrated by
Professor Lídio Ramires (2016).
We believe that restoring our ways of sharing knowledge in
order to defend the territory and build new educational
experiences stands in opposition to state policy, which aims to
maintain the order of the karaí and their top-down
interculturality. Thus, these experiences spring from Kaiowá and
Guarani struggles, in the face of the difficulties of
territorialization caused by agribusiness, which constantly tries
to colonize our ancestral lands.
I believe it is possible to think about interculturality on the
ground of the community, in such a way that the school engages
in dialogue with and learns from other pedagogical experiences
and our own spaces, which make possible a community
education built from traditional knowledge and practices, and
which open up other paths for interculturality outside of the
asymmetrical interculturality brought by the karaí, in which the
interests of the State and the colonizers prevail.
121
In this way, thinking about an education centered on theories
and practices that are specifically our own is indispensable for
the educational process to succeed in Indigenous school
institutions and in other educational spaces within the
communities. It is this relationship that guides the struggle for
an education that is truly ours, in which the pedagogical
principle of 'walking while asking questions,' together with the
original knowledge and practices of the peoples, wrests control
over teaching and learning in Indigenous schools from the hands
of the State.
What I propose to consider here as Intercultural Education is
that this construction be grounded in cosmology, in the socio-
territorial and ecological relations that arise through traditional
knowledge, as well as in respect for our way of life. These are the
elements that strengthen the struggle against the monoculture of
the mind and that recreate community spaces in defense of life
and of territories, seeking the construction of knowledge for life
and for bem viver.
122
